heuristics.rule: Counter 10–20% above initial offer as a baseline when you have no competing offer
heuristics.condition: When you have a single offer and the initial offer is at or near market rate
heuristics.action: Counter 10–12% above initial to leave room for the company to 'meet in the middle' at 5–8% above initial
heuristics.because: Recruiters are trained to move toward the middle — anchoring above your target lets the company feel they won while you land at your actual number

heuristics.rule: Counter 20–25% above initial when the offer is more than 15% below the levels.fyi median
heuristics.condition: When the initial offer is significantly below market rate
heuristics.action: Justify the counter with specific market data from levels.fyi framed as market alignment, not personal need
heuristics.because: A data-anchored counter is harder to dismiss and reframes the ask from 'I want more' to 'here's what the market looks like'

heuristics.rule: When you have a competing offer, counter to your target number directly — not 10–20% above initial
heuristics.condition: When you hold a competing offer
heuristics.action: Use the competing offer number as your anchor and ask the preferred company to match it
heuristics.because: The competing offer replaces the initial offer as the psychological anchor, removing the need to inflate your ask

heuristics.rule: Use precise numbers in late-round negotiation, round numbers early
heuristics.condition: When you are in round 2+ and both sides have narrowed, or when you have a specific data point to justify
heuristics.action: Switch from round numbers (anchoring signal) to precise numbers (research signal)
heuristics.because: Precise numbers like $192,400 signal you've done research; round numbers signal anchoring — each works best at different moments

heuristics.rule: Counter base first, then re-open equity separately after base is settled
heuristics.action: Isolate base in the first exchange; after base is settled, ask 'The equity grant — is that negotiable as well?'
heuristics.because: Mixing base and equity math in the first exchange muddies the negotiation and reduces your leverage on each component

heuristics.rule: When base is locked, pivot to signing bonus as it doesn't affect headcount budget
heuristics.condition: When the company says base is fixed and cannot move
heuristics.action: Ask for signing bonus increase framed as bridging the first-year comp gap
heuristics.because: Signing bonuses come from a different budget than base salary, so companies have more flexibility even after declaring base is final

heuristics.rule: Stop pushing after 'final offer' if it meets 90%+ of your target, but probe signing bonus first
heuristics.condition: When a company says 'this is our best and final offer'
heuristics.action: Accept if it meets 90%+ of target, but first test whether signing bonus has 5–10% more room
heuristics.because: 'Best and final' often still has signing bonus flexibility even when base is truly locked, and pushing further without new leverage risks damaging the relationship

heuristics.rule: Anchor your counter at or slightly above the levels.fyi median, not above the initial offer
heuristics.action: Start from market data, not from the initial offer, so your ask is framed as market alignment
heuristics.because: Framing the counter as market alignment rather than a personal demand makes it structurally harder for the recruiter to push back

decision_factors.factor: Distance of initial offer from market rate
decision_factors.why_it_matters: Determines how aggressive your counter should be — a below-market offer justifies a larger counter with market data as justification
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Pull levels.fyi data for the specific company, level, and location and compare to the initial offer

decision_factors.why_it_matters: Changes the entire counter structure — with a competing offer you counter to your target directly rather than anchoring above it
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Determine whether you have a written competing offer with a specific number you can reference

decision_factors.why_it_matters: Time pressure reduces your negotiating room and ability to generate competing offers
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Ask whether the offer has a hard deadline and how much time you have to respond

decision_factors.why_it_matters: Affects which levers are flexible — equity is often more negotiable at growth-stage companies while base and signing bonus are more flexible at large public companies
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Identify whether the company is pre-IPO, growth-stage, or a large public tech company and adjust which components you prioritize

decision_factors.why_it_matters: Determines whether to use round anchor numbers or precise research-backed numbers
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Track how many exchanges have occurred and how close both sides are to convergence

decision_factors.factor: Underlying reason for considering a move (in retention counter-offer scenarios)
decision_factors.why_it_matters: If the reason for leaving is not purely financial, a counter-offer that only addresses money will not solve the problem
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Ask yourself whether compensation was the primary driver or whether there are role, growth, or culture factors also at play

decision_factors.factor: Current tech salary growth market conditions
decision_factors.why_it_matters: Counter offer effectiveness remains high even as market conditions change, but baseline expectations should be calibrated accordingly
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Check current industry salary growth rates — as of 2025, tech salary growth has slowed to 1.6% vs. 3.5% in 2023

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Accepting a retention counter-offer from your current employer
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: 80% of people who accept counter-offers leave within 12 months anyway — the underlying reasons for considering leaving typically remain unresolved
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Anyone who is leaving for non-compensation reasons (growth ceiling, culture, management) but gets matched on salary

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Countering with a signing bonus instead of base when base is locked
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Signing bonus is immediate cash but does not compound — it does not raise the baseline for future raises, bonuses, or equity refreshes, which are all anchored to base salary
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Candidates planning to stay long-term at a company where annual raises and refresh grants are base-dependent

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Negotiating equity and base simultaneously in the first exchange
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Muddying the negotiation with total comp math reduces clarity and gives the recruiter room to trade off components against each other unfavorably
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Candidates who are less experienced at negotiation and do not realize that sequential negotiation of components preserves more leverage

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Continuing to push after a company says 'this is our final offer' without new leverage
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Risks damaging the relationship with the hiring team even if the offer is not withdrawn
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Candidates who have already met 90%+ of their target but push for marginal gains beyond the final offer threshold

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Disclosing the competing company name when using a competing offer as leverage
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Not required and potentially harmful — you have leverage from the number alone; disclosing the company name adds no benefit and may create complications
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Candidates negotiating between companies in the same industry or network where relationships between hiring teams exist

failure_patterns.pattern: Not countering at all due to fear of offer withdrawal
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Candidates overestimate withdrawal risk — the fear feels disproportionate because losing an offer feels catastrophic even though the statistical rate is only 6%
failure_patterns.consequence: Leaving an average of $27,000/year on the table — compounded over a career this is a significant wealth gap
warning_signs: Thinking 'I don't want to seem greedy'
Accepting the first offer without asking any questions about flexibility

failure_patterns.pattern: Countering based on personal need rather than market data
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Candidates frame their counter as 'I need more to pay rent/student loans' rather than anchoring to external market benchmarks
failure_patterns.consequence: Recruiter has an easy rebuttal since personal need is not their problem; data-anchored counters are structurally harder to dismiss
warning_signs: Using phrases like 'I was hoping for more'
Not pulling levels.fyi data before the negotiation conversation

failure_patterns.pattern: Negotiating all compensation components simultaneously in the first exchange
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Candidates want to optimize total comp and bundle everything together, not realizing this reduces leverage on each individual component
failure_patterns.consequence: Recruiter can trade off components against each other; candidate ends up with less on each lever than if negotiated sequentially
warning_signs: Sending a counter that includes a new base, new equity, and new signing bonus all at once
Framing the ask as 'I need total comp of X' without separating components

failure_patterns.pattern: Accepting 'base is fixed' without pivoting to signing bonus or equity
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Candidates interpret 'base is fixed' as 'the entire offer is fixed' and disengage from negotiation prematurely
failure_patterns.consequence: Leaves signing bonus and equity upside on the table — both of which come from different budget pools and remain negotiable even when base is locked
warning_signs: Immediately accepting after hearing 'base is our final number'
Not asking whether signing bonus or equity are separately negotiable

failure_patterns.pattern: Using the initial offer as the anchor for the counter rather than market data
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: The initial offer is salient and emotionally anchors the candidate, causing them to think in terms of percentage above what they were offered rather than what the market pays
failure_patterns.consequence: Counter lands below market rate even after negotiation, especially when the initial offer was significantly below median
warning_signs: Calculating counter as 'X% above what they offered' without checking levels.fyi
Not knowing the levels.fyi median before entering the negotiation

diagnostic_questions.question: Do you have a competing offer with a specific number?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether you have BATNA leverage that changes the entire counter structure
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Is the competing offer from a company you would genuinely consider joining? If yes, use that number as your direct anchor rather than a 10–20% counter above the initial offer.
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Are you in a position to generate a competing offer before the deadline? If not, proceed with market data as your anchor.

diagnostic_questions.question: How does the initial offer compare to the levels.fyi median for this specific company, level, and location?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: How aggressive your counter should be — a below-market offer justifies a 20–25% counter vs. 10–12% for a market-rate offer
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If the offer is more than 15% below median, prepare specific data points to justify the larger counter.
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If the offer is at or above median, a 10–12% counter is appropriate and a larger counter may face pushback without stronger justification.

diagnostic_questions.question: Is the offer exploding — do you have a hard deadline, and how much time do you have?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether you have time to generate competing offers or whether you must negotiate from your current position
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Prioritize negotiating the current offer aggressively since you cannot create additional leverage in the available time.
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Consider whether generating a competing offer before engaging in negotiation would strengthen your position.

diagnostic_questions.question: In a retention counter-offer scenario: what was the primary reason you considered leaving?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether a money-only counter-offer from the current employer will actually resolve the situation
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If compensation was the sole driver, a retention counter may work — but get specifics on timeline and structure.
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If role scope, growth ceiling, management, or culture were factors, a salary match does not address the underlying issue and the 80% within-12-months departure statistic becomes highly relevant.

diagnostic_questions.question: What round of negotiation are you in — is this your first counter or have you already exchanged multiple rounds?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether to use a high round-number anchor or a precise research-backed number
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If this is round 1, use a round number anchor above your target.
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If this is round 2 or later and both sides have narrowed, switch to a precise number to signal seriousness and research.

diagnostic_questions.question: Has the company said 'this is our best and final offer' on base?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether to stop pushing on base and pivot to signing bonus or equity as separate negotiable levers
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Ask specifically whether signing bonus is separately negotiable, framing it as bridging the first-year gap.
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Continue the base negotiation — 'final' has not been declared so room likely still exists.

industry_realities.common_belief: Asking for more after receiving an offer risks getting the offer pulled
industry_realities.actual_reality: Only 6% of offers are withdrawn after a counter — employers expect negotiation and withdrawal is almost exclusively reserved for candidates who are aggressive or disrespectful in tone, not those who simply ask for more
industry_realities.implication: The fear of withdrawal is statistically unjustified and should not be the reason you don't counter — the expected value of countering is strongly positive

industry_realities.common_belief: When a company says 'base is our final number,' the entire negotiation is over
industry_realities.actual_reality: Signing bonuses come from a different budget than base salary headcount and are almost always still negotiable even after base is declared final
industry_realities.implication: Always pivot to signing bonus when base is locked — $20K–$80K in signing bonus is standard at large tech companies for senior roles and does not require reopening base

industry_realities.common_belief: Accepting a retention counter-offer from your current employer solves the problem
industry_realities.actual_reality: 80% of people who accept counter-offers leave within 12 months anyway because the underlying non-compensation reasons for considering leaving remain unresolved
industry_realities.implication: Before accepting a retention counter-offer, explicitly assess whether the reason you considered leaving was purely financial — if not, the counter-offer is a temporary fix

industry_realities.common_belief: The right counter is a percentage above what the company offered
industry_realities.actual_reality: The right counter is anchored to market data (levels.fyi median for the specific company, level, and location), not to the initial offer — using the initial offer as your anchor can result in landing below market even after negotiation
industry_realities.implication: Always pull levels.fyi before building your counter number and start from market, not from the offer

industry_realities.common_belief: You need to disclose the competing company's name to use a competing offer as leverage
industry_realities.actual_reality: The competing offer number is the leverage — you are not required to disclose the company name and doing so adds no benefit while potentially creating complications
industry_realities.implication: When using a competing offer, share the number but decline to name the company if uncomfortable doing so

industry_realities.common_belief: Negotiating hard signals you are difficult to work with
industry_realities.actual_reality: 66% of candidates who negotiate get what they ask for — employers budget for negotiation and the process is expected, not penalized
industry_realities.implication: Framing your counter professionally and with market data is sufficient to preserve the relationship while capturing significant value

junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Counters as a percentage above the initial offer because that number is salient and emotionally anchoring
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Starts from the levels.fyi market median for the specific company, level, and location — the initial offer is irrelevant to the counter structure
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: A junior anchored to a below-market initial offer can negotiate hard and still land below market; a senior anchored to market data ensures the counter is calibrated correctly regardless of where the company started

junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Frames the ask in terms of personal need: 'I was hoping for more' or 'I need X to make this work'
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Frames the ask as market alignment: 'levels.fyi shows median for this level at X — I'd need to be at Y to align with market'
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Personal need framing gives the recruiter an easy rebuttal; market data framing is structurally harder to dismiss and signals research capability

junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Negotiates all components simultaneously — base, equity, and signing bonus in the same breath to maximize total comp
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Negotiates base first, then re-opens equity separately after base is settled, then uses signing bonus as a final lever if needed
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Simultaneous negotiation lets the recruiter trade off components against each other; sequential negotiation preserves leverage on each component independently

junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Accepts or disengages — interprets 'final' as meaning all negotiation is over
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Tests whether signing bonus has 5–10% more room before accepting, since signing bonus comes from a different budget than base
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Seniors capture additional value that juniors leave on the table by treating 'final on base' as 'final on everything'

junior_vs_senior_signals.dimension: Use of number precision as a negotiating signal
junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Uses either round numbers or precise numbers without strategic intent — picks a number and sticks to it
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Uses round numbers early (anchoring signal) and precise numbers late (research signal), switching deliberately based on which round of negotiation they are in
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: The right number format at the right time signals either anchoring intent or research depth — using them at the wrong time sends the wrong message to the recruiter

junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Evaluates the retention counter purely on whether the number matches or exceeds the external offer
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: First diagnoses whether the reason for considering leaving was purely financial — if not, recognizes that a money match does not solve the underlying problem
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Accepting a retention counter for non-financial reasons leads to departure within 12 months in 80% of cases — seniors avoid this trap by separating the compensation question from the root cause question
